title: LEBER OPTIC ATROPHY AND DYSTONIA
alt_titles: LEBER HEREDITARY OPTIC NEUROPATHY WITH DYSTONIA

intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that Leber optic atrophy and dystonia (LDYT) is caused by homoplasmic or heteroplasmic mutation in one of several mitochondrial genes encoding subunits of complex I: MTND6, MTND4, MTND1, or MTND3.

checks.explanation: The paper supports an ND1 (complex I) mutation causing LHON with dystonia and mentions earlier ND6 families. It does not cover the whole set of genes or say whether mutations are homoplasmic or heteroplasmic.

checks.claim: LDYT can be caused by mutation in the MTND6 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: The nucleotide G14459A mutation occurs in NADH dehydrogenase subunit 6, and has been suggested previously as the disease-causing mutation in Hispanic, African-American and Caucasian families of Leber's hereditary optic neuropathy (LHON) and/or dystonia.
checks.explanation: The abstract identifies the ND6 mutation in a family with LHON and dystonia.

paragraphs.text: Leber hereditary optic neuropathy and dystonia (LDYT) is a maternally inherited mitochondrial disorder. Affected people have different combinations of vision loss and progressive generalized dystonia (Wang et al., 2009). The dystonia is linked to bilateral, symmetric lesions of the basal ganglia, especially the putamen (Marsden et al., 1986; Jun et al., 1994). Within one family, some members have only optic neuropathy, some have only dystonia, and some have both (Novotny et al., 1986; De Vries et al., 1996).

checks.explanation: The title describes maternally inherited LHON and dystonia caused by an mtDNA mutation.

paragraphs.text: Marsden et al. (1986) described a disorder in 7 members of 2 families. In these patients, dystonia was associated to a variable degree with subacute visual loss or asymptomatic optic atrophy. CT scans showed striking bilateral symmetric lucencies, especially in the putamen. The authors considered that this might be a variant of Leigh disease, but noted considerable differences between these patients and those with pathologically proven Leigh disease. They stated that this condition must be excluded in all patients thought to have idiopathic dystonia, subacute visual failure similar to Leber optic neuropathy, or a combination of the two.

paragraphs.text: Jun et al. (1994) studied a severely affected child from a 5-generation Hispanic family with LHON and/or dystonia. They amplified the child's buffy coat mtDNA by PCR and sequenced more than 90% of it. The mtDNA had a Native American haplogroup D genotype and differed from the Cambridge reference sequence at 40 nucleotide positions. One variant was a G-to-A transition at nucleotide 14459 of the MTND6 gene, which changed a moderately conserved alanine to valine at residue 72 (A72V). The variant was absent from 38 Native American haplogroup D mtDNAs and from 108 Asian, 103 Caucasian, and 99 African mtDNAs. Six maternal relatives across 3 generations carried the mutation. One female relative with LHON was heteroplasmic. The authors concluded that this mutation was likely the cause of the disease.

paragraphs.text: In a large Dutch family with LHON and hereditary spastic dystonia, De Vries et al. (1996) found none of the mtDNA mutations previously reported in LHON. They sequenced the protein-coding mitochondrial genes and found 2 previously unreported mutations. The first was a heteroplasmic A-to-G transition at nucleotide 11696 in the MTND4 gene, resulting in a substitution between valine and isoleucine at amino acid 312. The second was a homoplasmic T-to-A change at nucleotide 14596 in the MTND6 gene, which substituted methionine for isoleucine at residue 26. A muscle biopsy showed severe complex I deficiency, which supported a link between these mtDNA mutations and the phenotype.

paragraphs.text: Spruijt et al. (2007) screened the complete mtDNA of a patient with LHON who did not carry any of the 3 primary LHON mutations. Other members of the patient's family had spastic dystonia. They found a pathogenic 3697G-A mutation in the MTND1 gene and determined its heteroplasmy level and biochemical effect; it appeared to be associated with an isolated complex I deficiency. The authors noted that this mutation can also cause MELAS syndrome and suggested that other genetic factors may contribute to its clinical expression.

paragraphs.text: Wang et al. (2009) studied a Chinese family with 18 patients with LDYT. They sequenced the entire mitochondrial genome with a resequencing microarray and found a 10197G-A mutation in the MTND3 gene on a haplogroup D4b background. The mutation substituted threonine for a highly conserved alanine at codon 47 (A47T). Quantitative analysis showed the mutation was homoplasmic in leukocytes of all affected individuals on the maternal side.

paragraphs.text: Spruijt et al. (2007) studied a family in which some members had LHON and others had spastic dystonia. In a patient with LHON who did not carry any of the 3 primary LHON mutations, they found a pathogenic 3697G-A mutation in the MTND1 gene. The mutation appeared to be associated with an isolated complex I deficiency.

paragraphs.text: In a Chinese family with 18 patients with LDYT, Wang et al. (2009) sequenced the entire mitochondrial genome with a resequencing microarray. They found a 10197G-A mutation in the MTND3 gene on a haplogroup D4b background, which substituted threonine for a highly conserved alanine at codon 47 (A47T). The mutation was homoplasmic in leukocytes of all affected individuals on the maternal side.
